catalog_quote: [p.24] In monomorphemic forms, main stress is on the initial syllable, with secondary stress on following odd-numbered syllables, though never on the final syllable, unless the final syllable is closed or contains a long vowel. The alternating strong-weak pattern within the morpheme is broken up by long vowels, which bear secondary stress in non-initial position. Primary stressed vowels are longer than other vowels, and there is often perceptible lengthening of post-stressed consonants; unstressed vowels are shorter than stressed vowels and often centralized, particularly in word-final position. Within each stress domain, assign quantity sensitive trochees from left to right respecting any lexical stress. b. If inchoative /-ba/ is stray, build a unary foot on it. c. new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is fixed on the word-initial syllable. Secondary stresses fall on following odd-numbered syllables (left-to-right trochees), skipping a light final syllable; heavy syllables (long vowels anywhere, closed syllables word-finally) attract secondary stress and interrupt the alternation; each morpheme of two or more moras starts a new stress domain in which the same rules re-apply.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Alternating on odd-numbered syllables after the initial, never on a light word-final syllable; long vowels (and word-final closed syllables) bear secondary stress in non-initial position; polymoraic suffixes/morphemes head their own stress domain; a light stressed syllable is destressed before a heavy secondary-stressed syllable (p.27). Examples p.25: mínga 'ant', pí'i 'uncle', yítka 'coals', ngúutu 'horse', úrdàa 'directly, soon'; p.27 ngútulùng 'kangaroo sausage', kúcidu-bà-nhàa 'starting to get hungry'.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically stressed suffixes: imperative -ga / -kà carries final secondary stress in the northern dialect even when the suffix is absent (cályabà 'be happy!', pp. 24, 28, 91, 94, 136); inchoative -ba is stressed though light (pp. 26-27); agentive -caa consistently attracts secondary stress (p. 60); proprietive -bagaa surfaces as bagàa (p. 65); compounds have primary stress on both formatives (pp. 70-71, 115); English stressed vowels are borrowed as Nhanda long vowels (p. 35). 'All long vowels in Nhanda attract stress' (p. 24).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level: 'A phonological word has exactly one main stress' (p. 45); stress domains are morphemes of >= 2 moras within the word; citation/monomorphemic forms tabulated in (15) p. 25 and multimorphemic in (16); phrasal pitch accent treated separately (p. 135: main stress in the phrase with phrase-final rise in yes/no questions). Phonetic correlates: primary-stressed vowels longer, post-tonic consonant lengthening, unstressed vowels shorter and centralized (p. 24).
new_statements.identity_note: Blevins 2001 describes Nhanda proper (the northern dialect, lower Murchison/Kalbarri to Northampton) almost entirely from one speaker, Mrs. Lucy Ryder; Blevins distinguishes three dialects (Nhanda north, Watchandi central, Amangu south) and notes that the lexically stressed imperative (-kà, final secondary stress) is a northern-dialect feature. Glottolog nhan1238 = the whole language; Austlang W14. Older sources spell it Nanda/Nhanta.

new_statements.quote: Word stress is usually on the first syllable, so it is the first part of the word that sounds the loudest. For example, in the English word 'radio', stress occurs on the first part of the word 'radio', in 'retire' stress occurs in the second part of the word.

new_statements.relation_note: The only stress sentence in the whole handbook is a region-wide generalisation (initial stress) covering WA Aboriginal languages, which is consistent with the catalog's initial-stress rule and Blevins 2001's 'main stress is on the initial syllable', but it is not a claim about Nhanda in particular; the Nhanda entry (4.3.10) is silent on stress. new_statements.rule_in_words: The handbook's general pronunciation guide states that, in Western Australian Aboriginal languages generally, word stress is usually on the first syllable. It makes no Nhanda-specific statement: entry 4.3.10 Nhanta is purely bibliographic (names, classification, speaker numbers, word lists, and a pointer to O'Grady, Voegelin & Voegelin 1966:119 as the only phonological/morphological sketch), with no phonology or stress content.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the statement is hedged as 'usually' and is region-wide, not language-specific
new_statements.identity_note: The handbook entry 4.3.10 covers 'Nhanta' (alternative names Eaw, Jau, Nanda, Watjandi), located south of the Murchison River near Northampton and Geraldton; it notes Morphy (1985) treats Amangu and Nhanta as the same language and Tindale lists Buluguda, Damala and Daguda as local hordes of Nhanta. No dialect is singled out for the stress generalisation, which is not language-specific at all.
